for-loop.title: for loops: do something for each item
for-loop.kid: Imagine a box of toys. A for loop takes the toys out one at a time, and for each one you do the same thing, like counting it or checking its colour.
how: A `for` loop visits every item of a list, every letter of a string, or every number in a range, in order. The loop variable (often `x`, `n` or `ch`) holds the current item on each pass.
Use it whenever the job is "look at everything once": add things up, find the biggest, count matches, build a new list.
Inside the loop you can stop early with `break` ("I found it, stop looking") or skip to the next item with `continue`.
for-loop.py:
total = 0
for n in [3, 5, 2]:
    total += n
print(total)
for-loop.watch: In JavaScript use `for (const x of list)` to get the items. `for (const x in list)` gives you the positions (as text), not the items.

range.title: Counting loops: range and i++
range.kid: It's like counting steps on a staircase: start at 0, go up one step at a time, and stop before a certain number.
how: `range(n)` gives the numbers `0, 1, 2, …, n-1`. `range(a, b)` starts at `a` and stops *before* `b`. `range(a, b, step)` jumps by `step` (use `-1` to count down).
In JavaScript the same thing is written `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)`: start at 0, keep going while `i < n`, add 1 after each pass.
Counting loops are how you visit positions (indexes) instead of items, which you need when you compare neighbours like `nums[i]` and `nums[i + 1]`.
range.watch: The end number is never included: `range(1, 4)` stops at 3. To include `n`, write `range(1, n + 1)`.

while-loop.title: while loops: keep going until something changes
while-loop.kid: Like eating cookies while there are still cookies on the plate. You don't know how many there are; you just stop when the plate is empty.
how: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It checks the condition before every pass.
Use it when you don't know in advance how many steps you need: chopping digits off a number until it's 0, moving two pointers until they meet, or following a linked list until you hit the end.
Something inside the loop must change, so the condition eventually becomes false. Otherwise the loop runs forever.
while-loop.py:
n = 1234
digits = 0
while n > 0:
    n //= 10
    digits += 1
print(digits)
while-loop.watch: Forgetting to update the variable in the condition (like `n` above) makes an infinite loop and the page hangs.

length.title: len() and .length: how many things
length.kid: It's counting how many beads are on a necklace.
how: `len(x)` in Python and `x.length` in JavaScript tell you how many items a list has, or how many characters a string has.
Positions go from `0` to `length - 1`, so the last item is at `len(x) - 1`. That's why loops over positions stop *before* the length.
An empty list or string has length 0, which is a handy way to check for "nothing here".
length.watch: `x[len(x)]` is one past the end: Python raises an IndexError and JavaScript quietly gives `undefined`.

indexing.title: Indexes: finding an item by its position
indexing.kid: Think of a row of numbered lockers starting at locker 0. To get what's in locker 2 you say "locker 2", not "the third locker".
how: Lists and strings are numbered from 0. `nums[0]` is the first item, `nums[1]` the second, and so on.
Python also counts from the end with negative numbers: `nums[-1]` is the last item, `nums[-2]` the one before. JavaScript uses `nums.at(-1)` or `nums[nums.length - 1]`.
You can change an item in a list by assigning to its position: `nums[0] = 9`. Python strings can't be changed in place, so you build a new one instead.
indexing.watch: Off-by-one errors: with 3 items the positions are 0, 1 and 2. There is no position 3.

append.title: Adding to a list: append and push
append.kid: Like adding a new carriage to the back of a toy train.
how: `list.append(x)` in Python and `array.push(x)` in JavaScript add `x` to the end of the list. The list grows by one.
A very common recipe: start with an empty list `[]`, loop over something, and append each answer you find. At the end you return the list.
Adding to the end is fast. Adding to the front (`insert(0, x)` / `unshift(x)`) has to shuffle everything along, so it's slow for big lists.
append.py:
squares = []
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)
append.watch: `append` changes the list itself and gives back `None`, so `result = result.append(x)` wipes out your list.

pop.title: Taking from a list: pop
pop.kid: Like taking the top plate off a stack of plates.
how: `pop()` removes the last item and gives it back to you. Python's `pop(0)` and JavaScript's `shift()` remove the first item instead.
Push and pop at the same end make a **stack**: the last thing in is the first thing out.
Popping from an empty list is an error in Python, and gives `undefined` in JavaScript, so check the list isn't empty first.
pop.watch: `pop(0)` / `shift()` on a long list is slow, because every other item moves up one. For a queue, use a deque.

slicing.title: Slicing: cutting out a piece
slicing.kid: Like cutting a few slices out of the middle of a loaf of bread. The loaf stays whole; you just get a copy of the slices.
how: `x[a:b]` in Python gives the items from position `a` up to, but not including, `b`. Leave a side empty to go to the edge: `x[:3]` is the first three, `x[3:]` is everything after.
JavaScript uses `x.slice(a, b)` for lists and strings, with the same rule.
A slice is a new copy. Changing it doesn't change the original.
slicing.watch: The end position isn't included: `word[0:3]` is 3 characters, positions 0, 1 and 2.

reverse.title: Reversing: back to front
reverse.kid: Like reading a word in a mirror: the last letter comes first.
how: In Python, `x[::-1]` is a reversed copy of a list or string (a slice that walks backwards). `reversed(x)` gives the items backwards for a loop.
In JavaScript, arrays have `.reverse()` (it changes the array itself). Strings don't, so the usual trick is `s.split("").reverse().join("")`.
Reversing is how you check palindromes: a word that reads the same both ways equals its own reverse.
reverse.watch: JavaScript's `.reverse()` changes the original array. Copy it first (`[...arr].reverse()`) if you still need the original.

split.title: split: chopping text into pieces
split.kid: Like cutting a string of sausages wherever there's a twist, so you get separate sausages.
how: `text.split()` in Python cuts text into a list of words at any spaces, and ignores extra spaces. `text.split(",")` cuts at every comma instead.
JavaScript's `text.split(" ")` cuts at single spaces. For "any amount of space", use `text.trim().split(/\s+/)`.
Splitting turns one string into a list, so you can count the words, loop over them or reverse them.
split.watch: `"".split(" ")` in JavaScript gives `[""]`, a list with one empty word, not an empty list.

join.title: join: gluing pieces back together
join.kid: Like threading beads onto a string, with the same knot between each bead.
how: `"-".join(parts)` in Python glues a list of strings together with `-` between them. JavaScript writes it the other way round: `parts.join("-")`.
`"".join(...)` glues with nothing in between. It's the fast way to build a long string from many small pieces.
Every piece must be a string in Python. Convert numbers first with `str(n)`.
join.watch: In Python the glue comes first: `"-".join(list)`, not `list.join("-")`.

case.title: Upper and lower case
case.kid: Like deciding that "Cat", "CAT" and "cat" all mean the same animal.
how: `text.lower()` / `text.toLowerCase()` makes every letter small; `upper()` / `toUpperCase()` makes them all capitals.
Lowering both sides first is the standard way to compare text without caring about capitals.
They give back a new string. The original is unchanged.
case.watch: `"A" == "a"` is false. If capitals shouldn't matter, lower both before comparing.

char-kind.title: Checking what kind of character it is
char-kind.kid: Like sorting a pile of things into "letters", "numbers" and "other stuff".
how: Python strings have checks: `ch.isalpha()` (a letter?), `ch.isdigit()` (0 to 9?), `ch.isalnum()` (letter or digit?), `ch.isspace()`.
JavaScript usually uses a small pattern test: `/[a-z]/i.test(ch)` for letters, `/[0-9]/.test(ch)` for digits, `/[a-z0-9]/i.test(ch)` for either.
These are handy for ignoring punctuation and spaces, as in "is this sentence a palindrome?".
char-kind.py:
for ch in "a1!":
    print(ch, ch.isalpha(), ch.isdigit())
char-kind.py_out:
a True False
1 False True
! False False
char-kind.js_out:
a true false
1 false true
! false false
char-kind.watch: Checking `ch in "aeiou"` only finds lowercase vowels. Lower the character first if capitals should count.

char-codes.title: Characters as numbers: ord and chr
char-codes.kid: Every letter secretly has a number, like a seat number in a cinema. 'a' sits in seat 97, 'b' in seat 98, and so on.
how: `ord("a")` / `"a".charCodeAt(0)` gives a character's number. `chr(97)` / `String.fromCharCode(97)` turns a number back into a character.
Letters are in order, so `ord(ch) - ord("a")` turns 'a' to 'z' into 0 to 25. That's perfect for a list of 26 counters, one per letter.
Shifting letters (as in a secret code) is just adding to the number and turning it back into a character.
char-codes.watch: Capital letters have different numbers ('A' is 65), so lower the text first if you use `- ord("a")`.

dict.title: Dictionaries and Maps: look things up by name
dict.kid: Like a real dictionary: you look up a word and find its meaning straight away, without reading every page.
how: A dictionary (Python `dict`, JavaScript `Map` or `{}`) stores **key → value** pairs. You ask for a key and get its value back instantly, however big it is.
The classic uses are counting (`counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1`) and remembering where you saw something (`seen[value] = index`).
`d.get(key, default)` gives a default instead of an error when the key is missing. In JavaScript, `map.get(key) ?? default` does the same.
dict.watch: `d[key]` on a missing key crashes in Python. Use `d.get(key, 0)` or check `key in d` first.

set.title: Sets: a bag with no duplicates
set.kid: Like a sticker album: each sticker has one spot, so if you get the same sticker again you don't add it twice.
how: A set keeps each value only once. Adding something already there does nothing.
Its superpower is the question "have I seen this before?": `x in seen` / `seen.has(x)` is instant, even with a million items. Doing that on a plain list means checking every item.
Turning a list into a set and comparing lengths tells you whether the list had duplicates.
set.py:
seen = set()
for n in [4, 1, 4, 2]:
    seen.add(n)
print(len(seen), 4 in seen)
set.watch: `{}` makes an empty *dictionary* in Python. An empty set is `set()`.

membership.title: Is it in there? (in, includes, has)
membership.kid: Like asking "is my friend in this room?" and getting a yes or a no.
how: Python's `x in container` answers yes or no for lists, strings, sets and dictionary keys. JavaScript uses `list.includes(x)`, `text.includes(sub)`, `set.has(x)` and `map.has(key)`.
Speed depends on the container: sets and dictionaries answer instantly, while lists and strings check item by item.
`not in` (Python) and `!list.includes(x)` (JavaScript) ask the opposite question.
membership.py:
vowels = "aeiou"
print("e" in vowels, "z" in vowels)
membership.watch: Checking `in` on a long list inside a loop is slow. Make a set first if you'll ask many times.

unpack.title: Unpacking and swapping in one line
unpack.kid: Like two kids swapping toys at the same moment, so nobody is ever left holding nothing.
how: `a, b = 1, 2` sets two variables at once. `a, b = b, a` swaps them without a temporary helper variable.
JavaScript does the same with brackets: `[a, b] = [b, a]`.
You'll see it everywhere in two-pointer code, Fibonacci-style updates (`a, b = b, a + b`) and when a function returns two things.
unpack.py:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
unpack.watch: Doing it in two lines (`a = b` then `b = a`) loses the old `a`. Both sides must change at once.

enumerate.title: Getting the position and the item together
enumerate.kid: Like a teacher calling the register: "Number 1, Ada. Number 2, Ben." You get the number and the name together.
how: `for i, x in enumerate(items):` gives you each item `x` and its position `i` at the same time.
JavaScript: `items.forEach((x, i) => …)` or `for (const [i, x] of items.entries())`.
You need both when the answer is a position ("return the index of …") but the decision depends on the value.
enumerate.py:
for i, name in enumerate(["Ada", "Ben"]):
    print(i, name)
enumerate.watch: enumerate starts at 0. Use `enumerate(items, start=1)` if you want to count from 1.

zip.title: zip: walking two lists side by side
zip.kid: Like a zipper: the left teeth and right teeth come together in pairs, one pair at a time.
how: `zip(a, b)` pairs the first item of `a` with the first of `b`, the second with the second, and so on.
It stops at the shorter list. JavaScript has no zip, so you loop over positions: `for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++)` and use `a[i]` and `b[i]`.
Handy for comparing two lists or strings letter by letter.
zip.py:
for name, score in zip(["Ada", "Ben"], [90, 85]):
    print(name, score)
zip.watch: Extra items in the longer list are silently skipped.

min-max.title: Smallest and biggest: min and max
min-max.kid: Like lining your friends up by height and pointing at the shortest and the tallest.
how: `min(a, b)` / `max(a, b)` give the smaller or bigger of two values. `min(list)` / `max(list)` look through a whole list.
JavaScript: `Math.min(a, b)`, `Math.max(...list)` (the `...` spreads the list out).
A very common pattern is a running best: `best = max(best, current)` inside a loop.
min-max.py:
best = 0
for n in [3, 9, 4]:
    best = max(best, n)
print(best, min([3, 9, 4]))
min-max.watch: Starting a running maximum at 0 is wrong if every number can be negative. Start at the first item, or at minus infinity.

sum.title: Adding everything up
sum.kid: Like emptying your piggy bank and counting all the coins together.
how: `sum(list)` adds up every number in a Python list.
JavaScript uses `list.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0)`: start at 0 and add each number in turn.
Both give 0 for an empty list, which is usually exactly what you want.
sum.watch: In JavaScript, always give `reduce` its starting value (the `0`), or an empty list throws an error.

sorting.title: Sorting: putting things in order
sorting.kid: Like lining up books from shortest to tallest so you can find things quickly.
how: `sorted(list)` gives a new sorted list; `list.sort()` sorts the list itself. Add `reverse=True` for biggest first, or `key=` to sort by something else, like `key=len` for word length.
JavaScript's `.sort()` compares things as **text** by default, so numbers need a rule: `nums.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.
Sorting first often makes a hard problem easy: duplicates end up next to each other, and two pointers can walk from both ends.
sorting.watch: See the JavaScript example: without `(a, b) => a - b`, numbers sort as text, so 10 comes before 2.

lambda.title: Tiny functions written in one line
lambda.kid: Like a sticky note with one quick instruction on it, such as "compare by length".
how: `lambda x: x * 2` in Python and `x => x * 2` in JavaScript make a small function without giving it a name.
You'll mostly see them handed to other functions, telling them *how* to do something: how to sort (`key=lambda p: p[1]`), what to keep (`filter`) or how to change each item (`map`).
If the instruction needs more than one line, write a normal function instead.
lambda.js:
const pairs = [["Ben", 3], ["Ada", 1]];
console.log(pairs.sort((a, b) => a[1] - b[1]));
lambda.watch: A Python lambda can only hold one expression, with no `if` blocks or loops inside.

comprehension.title: Building a list in one line
comprehension.kid: Like saying "give me a cup of juice for every kid who is thirsty" instead of going kid by kid.
how: Python: `[x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0]` makes a new list in one line: take each `x`, keep it only if the condition holds, and put in `x * 2`.
JavaScript chains `filter` (keep some) and `map` (change each): `nums.filter(x => x > 0).map(x => x * 2)`.
It's the same as a loop with `append`, just shorter. Use whichever you find easier to read.
comprehension.py:
nums = [3, -1, 4]
print([x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0])
comprehension.watch: `[[0] * 3] * 3` makes three references to the *same* row. Build grids with `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`.

modulo.title: % (modulo): the remainder after dividing
modulo.kid: If you share 7 sweets between 3 friends, each gets 2 and 1 is left over. That leftover 1 is `7 % 3`.
how: `a % b` is what's left after dividing `a` by `b` as many whole times as possible.
`n % 2 == 0` means `n` is even. `n % 10` is the last digit of `n`. `i % len(list)` wraps around to the start, like a clock.
Divisibility questions ("is it a multiple of 3?") are always `% 3 == 0`.
modulo.watch: With negative numbers Python and JavaScript disagree: `-7 % 3` is 2 in Python and -1 in JavaScript.

floor-div.title: // and Math.floor: dividing without the leftover
floor-div.kid: Sharing 7 sweets between 3 friends: everyone gets 2 whole sweets. Nobody gets 2.33 sweets.
how: `a // b` in Python divides and throws away the part after the decimal point (it rounds down). `7 // 2` is 3.
JavaScript's `/` always gives decimals, so write `Math.floor(a / b)`. `Math.trunc` rounds toward zero instead, which differs for negatives.
`n // 10` chops the last digit off a number. `(lo + hi) // 2` finds the middle position in binary search.
floor-div.watch: Plain `/` in Python gives a decimal (`7 / 2` is 3.5), and positions must be whole numbers.

infinity.title: Infinity: a start value nothing can beat
infinity.kid: If you're looking for the smallest number, start with "bigger than anything". The first real number you see is smaller, so it takes over.
how: `float("inf")` in Python and `Infinity` in JavaScript are bigger than every number. `-inf` / `-Infinity` are smaller than every number.
Start a running minimum at infinity and a running maximum at minus infinity, then compare as you go.
If the answer is still infinity at the end, nothing was found, which is a handy way to return -1 or 0 for "impossible".
infinity.py:
best = float("inf")
for n in [7, 3, 5]:
    best = min(best, n)
print(best)
infinity.watch: Remember to turn "still infinity" into the answer the problem asks for (often -1) before returning.

none.title: None and null: nothing there
none.kid: Like an empty parking space: it's a real space, there just isn't a car in it right now.
how: `None` in Python and `null` in JavaScript mean "no value". They mark the end of a linked list, a missing child in a tree, or "not found yet".
Check for it with `x is None` (Python) or `x === null` (JavaScript) before using the value.
JavaScript also has `undefined`, which you get when something was never set.
none.js:
const node = null;
if (node === null) console.log("empty");
none.watch: Reading `node.next` when `node` is None/null crashes. Check first.

convert.title: Turning numbers into text and back
convert.kid: The number 42 and the word "42" look the same on paper, but one you can do maths with and the other you can read letter by letter.
how: `str(42)` / `String(42)` turns a number into text, so you can loop over its digits. `int("42")` / `Number("42")` turns text back into a number.
Mixing them up causes surprises: in JavaScript `"4" + 2` is `"42"`, because + joins text.
`int("7")` is a quick way to turn a single digit character into a number.
convert.watch: Text "9" plus number 1 is an error in Python and "91" in JavaScript. Convert first.

any-all.title: any and all: checking a whole list at once
how: `any(...)` is true if at least one item passes. `all(...)` is true only if every item passes.
JavaScript: `list.some(x => …)` and `list.every(x => …)`.
Both stop as soon as they know the answer, so they're as fast as a loop with `break`.
any-all.py:
nums = [2, 4, 7]
print(any(n % 2 for n in nums), all(n > 0 for n in nums))
any-all.js:
const nums = [2, 4, 7];
console.log(nums.some(n => n % 2), nums.every(n => n > 0));
any-all.watch: `all` of an empty list is True: nobody broke the rule, because there's nobody.

abs.title: abs: distance from zero
abs.kid: Whether you walk 3 steps forward or 3 steps back, you still walked 3 steps.
how: `abs(-3)` / `Math.abs(-3)` is 3. It drops the minus sign.
Use it for "how far apart are these two numbers?": `abs(a - b)`, whichever is bigger.

deque.title: Queues: first in, first out
deque.kid: Like the line at an ice cream van: whoever joined first gets served first.
how: A queue adds at the back and takes from the front. Python's `collections.deque` does both ends quickly: `append` to join, `popleft` to serve.
JavaScript has no built-in deque. Use an array and a `head` position that moves forward, or `shift()` for small inputs.
Queues power breadth-first search: visit things in the order you found them, nearest first.
deque.py:
from collections import deque
q = deque([1, 2])
q.append(3)
print(q.popleft(), list(q))
deque.watch: `list.pop(0)` in Python works but is slow for big lists. Use `deque.popleft()`.

heapq.title: Heaps: always grab the smallest quickly
heapq.kid: Like a magic bag that always hands you the smallest marble first, however you threw them in.
how: A heap keeps its smallest item ready at the top. Adding (`heappush`) and taking the smallest (`heappop`) are both fast, even with lots of items.
Python's `heapq` works on a plain list. For the *biggest* first, push negative numbers and flip the sign back when you pop.
JavaScript has no built-in heap. The solutions here either sort or write a small heap class.
heapq.py:
import heapq
h = []
for n in [5, 1, 3]:
    heapq.heappush(h, n)
print(heapq.heappop(h), heapq.heappop(h))
heapq.watch: A heap is not fully sorted. Only the top item (`h[0]`) is guaranteed to be the smallest.

bisect.title: bisect: finding where something fits in a sorted list
bisect.kid: Like slotting a new book onto an already-sorted shelf: you jump to the middle, then the middle of the half, until you find its spot.
how: `bisect_left(sorted_list, x)` gives the position where `x` would go to keep the list sorted. It uses binary search, so it's fast even for huge lists.
JavaScript has no built-in version; you write the binary-search loop yourself (see the Binary search card).
bisect.py:
from bisect import bisect_left
print(bisect_left([1, 3, 5, 7], 5), bisect_left([1, 3, 5, 7], 4))
bisect.watch: The list must already be sorted, or the answer is meaningless.

bits.title: Bits: numbers as rows of on/off switches
bits.kid: Every number is secretly a row of light switches that are either on (1) or off (0). 5 is `101`: on, off, on.
how: `a & b` keeps a switch on only where both are on. `a | b` turns it on where either is. `a ^ b` (XOR) turns it on where they're *different*.
`x << 1` slides every switch left one place (doubling the number); `x >> 1` slides right (halving it, rounding down).
Two famous tricks: `x ^ x` is 0, so XOR-ing everything cancels out the pairs. `n & (n - 1)` switches off the lowest 'on' switch.
bits.watch: `^` is not "to the power of". Powers are `**` in both languages.

class.title: Classes: designing your own kind of thing
class.kid: A class is a cookie cutter. Each cookie you make with it (an object) has the same shape, but its own sprinkles (its own data).
how: A class bundles data (`self.items` / `this.items`) with the actions that use it (methods such as `push` or `get`).
The setup method, `__init__` in Python and `constructor` in JavaScript, runs once when the object is created, to get its data ready.
Design problems ask you to write such a class: the tests create one and call its methods in order, checking each answer.
class.watch: Inside a method, use `self.` / `this.` to reach the object's data. A bare `n` is a different, local variable.

big-o.title: Big-O: how the work grows
big-o.kid: Saying hello to everyone in a room takes longer when more people come. Big-O describes *how much* longer.
how: **O(1)**: same work however big the input, like looking at the first item. **O(n)**: one quick look at each item, like a single loop. **O(n²)**: every item compared with every other one, two nested loops.
**O(log n)**: each step throws away half the work, like binary search. A million items need only about 20 steps.
The constraints line tells you what's fast enough. With up to 100,000 items, O(n²) is about 10 billion steps (too slow), so look for O(n) or O(n log n).
big-o.py:
nums = list(range(1000))
steps = 0
for a in nums:
    steps += 1
print(steps)
big-o.watch: Hidden loops count too: `x in list`, `list.index`, `list.pop(0)` and slicing inside a loop each walk the list again.

hashing.title: Hash tables: remember what you've seen
hashing.kid: Like keeping a notebook while you search: every time you see something, you write it down, so you never have to search for it again.
how: Many problems become one pass if you remember things as you go. Put each value (or count, or position) into a dictionary or set.
Then "have I seen the number that would complete my pair?" is an instant lookup instead of a second loop.
This trades a little memory for a big speed-up: usually from O(n²) down to O(n).
hashing.watch: Check whether you've seen it *before* you add the current item, or every item looks like a repeat of itself.

two-pointers.title: Two pointers: two fingers walking the list
two-pointers.kid: Put one finger at the start of a line of kids and one at the end, and walk them toward each other, comparing as you go.
how: Keep two positions, often `left = 0` and `right = len - 1`. Each step, look at both, then move one of them inward.
On a **sorted** list, if the pair's sum is too small, move `left` right to grow it; if it's too big, move `right` left. Each step rules something out, so it's one pass.
Another version has both fingers start at the left: a slow one marks where to write and a fast one reads ahead. That's how you remove items in place.
two-pointers.py:
s = "racecar"
left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
ok = True
while left < right:
    if s[left] != s[right]:
        ok = False
    left += 1
    right -= 1
print(ok)
two-pointers.watch: Use `while left < right`, not `<=`, when the two pointers mustn't look at the same item.

fast-slow.title: Fast and slow pointers: the tortoise and the hare
fast-slow.kid: A tortoise and a hare race on a track. If the track is a loop, the hare eventually laps the tortoise and they meet.
how: Move one pointer one step at a time and another two steps at a time.
If they ever meet, there's a cycle. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is exactly in the middle.
It needs no extra memory, unlike remembering every node you've visited.
fast-slow.py:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
slow = fast = 0
while fast + 1 < len(nums):
    slow += 1
    fast += 2
print(nums[slow])
fast-slow.watch: Check that `fast` and `fast.next` both exist before jumping two steps.

sliding-window.title: Sliding window: a frame that slides along
sliding-window.kid: Look at a long train through a window that shows 3 carriages at a time. As the train moves, one carriage leaves the window and a new one comes in.
how: Keep a window from `left` to `right` over the list or string. Grow it by moving `right`; shrink it by moving `left` when it breaks the rule (too many repeats, sum too big…).
Update what you know (a running sum, a count of letters) as items enter and leave, instead of recounting the whole window each time.
Each item enters once and leaves once, so the whole thing is O(n).
sliding-window.py:
nums, k = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3
window = sum(nums[:k])
best = window
for right in range(k, len(nums)):
    window += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
    best = max(best, window)
print(best)
sliding-window.watch: When the window shrinks, undo exactly what was added when that item came in.

prefix-sum.title: Prefix sums: running totals
prefix-sum.kid: Like a scoreboard that shows the total so far after every round. To know how many points were scored in rounds 3 to 5, subtract two totals.
how: Build a list where each spot holds the sum of everything up to there: `prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]`.
Then the sum of any stretch from `i` to `j` is `prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]`: one subtraction instead of a loop.
Paired with a dictionary of totals seen so far, it answers "how many stretches add up to k?" in one pass.
prefix-sum.py:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1]
prefix = [0]
for n in nums:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + n)
print(prefix, prefix[3] - prefix[1])
prefix-sum.watch: The prefix list is one longer than the input. Start it with 0.

stack.title: Stacks: last in, first out
stack.kid: Like a stack of pancakes: you add to the top and eat from the top. The last pancake added is the first one eaten.
how: Push things onto a list with `append` / `push`; take the most recent off with `pop`.
Perfect for matching things: on an opening bracket, push it; on a closing bracket, pop and check it matches.
Also for "undo" and for anything where the most recent item matters most.
stack.watch: Check the stack isn't empty before popping, and that it *is* empty at the end.

monotonic-stack.title: Monotonic stacks: waiting for something bigger
monotonic-stack.kid: Kids queue up holding a balloon each. When a kid with a bigger balloon arrives, everyone with a smaller balloon finally finds out who beats them, and leaves.
how: Keep a stack whose values only go down (or only up). Before pushing a new item, pop everything it beats.
Each popped item has just found its "next greater element": the new item.
Every item is pushed once and popped once, so it's O(n) even though it looks like a nested loop.
monotonic-stack.py:
nums = [2, 1, 3]
answer = [-1] * len(nums)
stack = []
for i, n in enumerate(nums):
    while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < n:
        answer[stack.pop()] = n
    stack.append(i)
print(answer)
monotonic-stack.watch: Store positions on the stack, not values, when the answer needs to know where things are.

binary-search.title: Binary search: halve the search every time
binary-search.kid: Guessing a number from 1 to 100: say 50. "Too high!" Now it's 1 to 49, so say 25. Every guess throws away half of what's left.
how: On a **sorted** list, look at the middle. If it's too small, the answer must be to the right; if too big, to the left. Throw away the wrong half and repeat.
Keep `lo` and `hi`, compute `mid = (lo + hi) // 2`, and move `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`. Stop when `lo > hi`.
It's O(log n): a million items need about 20 checks. It also works on answers ("what's the smallest speed that works?") whenever bigger always means easier.
binary-search.watch: Off-by-one is the classic bug: decide whether `hi` is included, and keep `lo <= hi` and `hi = mid - 1` consistent with that.

linked-list.title: Linked lists: a treasure hunt of nodes
linked-list.kid: Like a treasure hunt: each clue says something, then tells you where the next clue is. The last clue says "the end".
how: Each node holds a value (`val`) and a pointer to the next node (`next`). The last node's `next` is None/null. You only get the first node, the `head`.
To walk it: `node = head`, then `while node:` do something and move on with `node = node.next`.

Changing a list means redirecting `next` pointers. A dummy node in front of the head saves special cases when the head itself might change. On this site the examples show a linked list as a plain list like `[1, 2, 3]`.
linked-list.watch: Save `node.next` in a variable before you change it, or you lose the rest of the list.

tree.title: Trees: a family tree of nodes
tree.kid: Like a family tree upside down: one grandparent at the top (the root), each person has up to two children below them (left and right), and the people with no children are leaves.
how: Each node has a value and `left` / `right` children, which may be None/null. You're given the `root`.
Most tree problems use the same move: solve it for the left child, solve it for the right child, and combine the two answers. That's recursion.

In a **binary search tree** everything on the left is smaller and everything on the right is bigger, so you can find a value by going left or right, like binary search. On this site the examples show a tree level by level, like `[3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]`.
tree.watch: Always handle the empty tree (None/null) first. It's the base case that stops the recursion.

recursion.title: Recursion: a function that calls itself
recursion.kid: Russian dolls: to count the dolls, open one, and count the dolls inside it the same way, until you reach the tiny one that doesn't open.
how: A recursive function solves a big problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem.
It needs a **base case**, the tiny version you can answer straight away (like `n == 0` or an empty node). Without it, it never stops.
Each call waits for the smaller one to finish, then uses its answer. Python stops at about 1,000 nested calls, so very deep inputs need a loop instead.
recursion.watch: Make sure every call gets closer to the base case, or it runs until it crashes.

dfs.title: Depth-first search: go as deep as you can first
dfs.kid: Exploring a maze by always taking the first turn, going as far as you can, and only backing up when you hit a dead end.
how: From a starting point, visit a neighbour, then its neighbour, and so on, going deep before going wide. Recursion (or a stack) remembers where to come back to.
Mark places as visited so you never go round in circles.
Use it to explore everything connected to a starting point: islands in a grid, all paths in a tree, every room in a building.
dfs.watch: On a grid or graph with loops, mark a cell visited *before* exploring its neighbours.

bfs.title: Breadth-first search: ripples in a pond
bfs.kid: Drop a stone in a pond: the ripple reaches everything 1 step away first, then everything 2 steps away, and so on.
how: Use a queue. Start with the first place in it. Repeatedly take the front item, then add its unvisited neighbours to the back.
Because it spreads one layer at a time, the first time you reach something is by the **shortest path** (when every step costs the same).
To work layer by layer ("level order"), handle exactly `len(queue)` items in each round.
bfs.watch: Mark a place as visited when you *add* it to the queue, not when you take it out, or it gets added many times.

grid.title: Grids: lists inside a list
grid.kid: Like a chessboard or a spreadsheet: you find a square by its row and its column.
how: A grid is a list of rows, and each row is a list. `grid[r][c]` is the cell in row `r`, column `c`.
The number of rows is `len(grid)` and the number of columns is `len(grid[0])`.
The four neighbours of a cell are `(r-1, c)`, `(r+1, c)`, `(r, c-1)` and `(r, c+1)`. Always check a neighbour is inside the grid before using it.
grid.watch: Row first, then column: `grid[r][c]`, not `grid[x][y]` like on a maths graph.

graph.title: Graphs: dots joined by lines
graph.kid: Like a map of towns joined by roads. Towns are nodes and roads are edges.
how: Problems usually give the roads as a list of pairs, like `[[0, 1], [1, 2]]`. Turn it into an **adjacency list**: for each town, the list of towns it connects to.
Then explore it with DFS or BFS, remembering which towns you've visited.
Roads can be one-way (directed) or two-way. For two-way roads, add each pair in both directions.
graph.watch: Towns with no roads still exist. Create an empty list for every town, not just the ones in `edges`.

heap-pattern.title: Top-k with a heap
heap-pattern.kid: To keep the 3 tallest kids in a crowd, hold a small group of 3. When someone taller comes along, the shortest in your group leaves.
how: Keep a min-heap of size `k`. Push each new item; if the heap grows past `k`, pop the smallest.
At the end the heap holds the `k` biggest items, and its top (`h[0]`) is the k-th biggest.
That's O(n log k), much faster than sorting everything when `k` is small.
heap-pattern.py:
import heapq
h = []
for n in [5, 1, 9, 3, 7]:
    heapq.heappush(h, n)
    if len(h) > 2:
        heapq.heappop(h)
print(h[0])
heap-pattern.watch: For the k *smallest*, flip it: keep a max-heap (push negatives in Python).

backtracking.title: Backtracking: try, and undo if it doesn't work
backtracking.kid: Like trying on outfits: put on a shirt, try a pair of trousers with it, take the trousers off, try the next pair. When you've tried them all, swap the shirt.
how: Build an answer one choice at a time. After each choice, go deeper and make the next one.
When the answer is complete, save a **copy** of it. Then undo the last choice (`pop`) and try the next option.
It explores every possibility, so it's slow for big inputs, but the problems that need it keep inputs small.
backtracking.py:
result, path = [], []
def choose(start):
    result.append(path[:])
    for n in range(start, 3):
        path.append(n)
        choose(n + 1)
        path.pop()
choose(0)
print(result)
backtracking.watch: Save `path[:]` / `[...path]`, a copy. Saving `path` itself saves the same list over and over, and it ends up empty.

dp.title: Dynamic programming: remember small answers to build big ones
dp.kid: To know how many ways you can climb 5 stairs (1 or 2 at a time), first work out 1 stair, then 2, then 3… writing each answer down so you never work it out twice.
how: Break the problem into smaller versions of itself, solve the smallest first, and store every answer in a list (or a dictionary).
Each new answer is built from answers you already have. For stairs: `ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + ways[i - 2]`.
The hard part is deciding what one number means, like "`dp[i]` = the best I can do with the first `i` items". Once you have that, the rule usually follows.
dp.py:
n = 5
ways = [1, 1] + [0] * (n - 1)
for i in range(2, n + 1):
    ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + ways[i - 2]
print(ways[n])
dp.watch: Get the starting values (the base cases, like `ways[0]` and `ways[1]`) right. Everything else is built on them.

greedy.title: Greedy: take the best choice right now
greedy.kid: Paying 40p with the fewest coins: grab the biggest coin that fits (20p), then again (20p). Done.
how: At every step, make the choice that looks best right now, and never go back on it.
It's fast and simple, but it only works when you can convince yourself a locally best choice never spoils the final answer.
Greedy problems often sort first, for example by end time for intervals.
greedy.py:
coins, amount = [20, 10, 5], 40
used = 0
for c in coins:
    used += amount // c
    amount %= c
print(used)
greedy.watch: Greedy can be wrong. With coins [4, 3, 1] and amount 6, greedy gives 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 is 2. Check with a tricky example.

trie.title: Tries: a tree of letters
trie.kid: Like a word game where you follow letters down a branching path: c → a → t spells "cat", and c → a → r spells "car". Words starting the same share the start of the path.
how: Each node is a small dictionary from a letter to the next node, plus a flag saying "a word ends here".
To add a word, walk its letters, creating nodes as needed. To search, walk them and check the flag at the end.
"Does any word start with …" becomes fast: just walk the prefix.
trie.watch: "car" being a prefix of "cart" doesn't make it a word. That's what the end-of-word flag is for.
